items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the thin, rigid outer layer of the Earth, 5-10 km thick under oceans and up to about 70 km under continents”?
items.answer: Crust
items.markingKey: Crust: the thin, rigid outer layer of the Earth, 5-10 km thick under oceans and up to about 70 km under continents. [1]

items.stem: Explain how a mid-ocean ridge is formed.
items.answer: Plates move apart at a constructive boundary; pressure is reduced so the mantle partially melts; magma rises and cools to form new basaltic crust; hot, buoyant crust is raised to form a ridge.
items.markingKey: plates diverge [1]; magma rises and solidifies [1]; new crust uplifted into a ridge [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why volcanoes form at destructive plate boundaries.
items.answer: The subducting oceanic plate is heated and releases water, which lowers the melting point of the mantle above; magma forms, rises through the overlying plate and erupts.
items.markingKey: subduction [1]; melting / water lowers melting point [1]; magma rises to the surface [1] [3]

items.stem: Fig. 1.1 is a cross-section across the west coast of South America, showing the Nazca plate moving east towards the South American plate, an ocean trench, and the Andes mountains with volcanoes. Describe how the mountains were formed.
items.answer: Compression as the plates converge folds and thickens the continental crust, and volcanic material adds to it, forming fold mountains.
items.markingKey: compression / folding [1]; thickening and volcanic addition [1] [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.1 is a cross-section across the west coast of South America, showing the Nazca plate moving east towards the South American plate, an ocean trench, and the Andes mountains with volcanoes. (a) Name the type of plate boundary shown. (b) Describe how the mountains were formed.
items.answer: (a) Destructive (convergent, subduction) boundary. (b) Compression as the plates converge folds and thickens the continental crust, and volcanic material adds to it, forming fold mountains.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) compression / folding [1]; thickening and volcanic addition [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Mumbai is studying a cross-section of a destructive plate boundary where oceanic crust meets continental crust, such as the boundary off Chile. (a) Suggest why earthquakes here occur at a range of depths. (b) Describe how the mountains were formed.
items.answer: (a) Friction between the plates causes earthquakes along the sloping subducting slab (Benioff zone), shallow near the trench and deeper inland. (b) Compression as the plates converge folds and thickens the continental crust, and volcanic material adds to it, forming fold mountains.
items.markingKey: (a) friction / stress along slab [1]; slab slopes so foci get deeper inland [1] [2] (b) compression / folding [1]; thickening and volcanic addition [1] [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Earthquakes only happen at destructive plate boundaries.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Earthquakes occur at all boundaries, including constructive and conservative ones (e.g. the San Andreas Fault); intraplate earthquakes also occur.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.1 is a cross-section across the west coast of South America, showing the Nazca plate moving east towards the South American plate, an ocean trench, and the Andes mountains with volcanoes. (a) Explain why an ocean trench forms at this boundary. (b) Explain the formation of the volcanoes.
items.answer: (a) The denser oceanic plate bends down and sinks beneath the continental plate, creating a deep trench where it descends. (b) The subducted plate is heated at depth and releases water; mantle melts; magma rises through the continental crust and erupts.
items.markingKey: (a) denser oceanic plate [1]; sinks / subducts, forming trench [1] [2] (b) heat / water release [1]; melting [1]; magma rises [1] [3]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “rock formed when molten magma or lava cools and crystallises”?
items.answer: Igneous rock
items.markingKey: Igneous rock: rock formed when molten magma or lava cools and crystallises. [1]

items.stem: Explain why the rock cycle is described as a cycle.
items.answer: Rocks are continually changed from one type to another: igneous rocks are weathered into sediments that form sedimentary rocks, which may be metamorphosed or melted to form magma and new igneous rock; there is no start or end.
items.markingKey: changes between types [1]; named linking processes [1]; continuous / no start or end [1] [3]

items.stem: Describe how a sedimentary rock such as sandstone forms.
items.answer: Rock is weathered and eroded; sediment is transported and deposited in layers (e.g. in seas); the weight of overlying layers compacts it; minerals in water cement the grains together.
items.markingKey: weathering and erosion [1]; deposition in layers [1]; compaction and cementation [1] [3]

items.stem: A geology student in Doha collected three rock samples. Sample A has large interlocking crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica. Sample B is made of rounded sand grains in layers and contains a fossil shell. Sample C has very fine grains and splits into thin flat sheets. Explain why sample B contains fossils.
items.answer: It formed from sediment deposited in layers, which buried organisms; low temperatures preserved their remains, which were lithified with the sediment.
items.markingKey: deposition burying organisms [1]; no melting / preserved [1] [2]

items.stem: A geology student in Santiago collected three rock samples. Sample A has large interlocking crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica. Sample B is made of rounded sand grains in layers and contains a fossil shell. Sample C has very fine grains and splits into thin flat sheets. (a) Explain how the large crystals in sample A formed. (b) Describe how sample C could have formed from a sedimentary rock.
items.answer: (a) Magma cooled slowly underground, giving time for large crystals to grow. (b) Shale or mudstone was subjected to high pressure (and heat), e.g. at a plate boundary; minerals realigned in parallel, so it splits into sheets (slate).
items.markingKey: (a) slow cooling [1]; underground / intrusive [1] [2] (b) pressure / heat [1]; realignment / cleavage [1] [2]

items.stem: Elena argues that the rock cycle is mainly driven by plate tectonics. Discuss this view, referring to named examples. In your answer you should consider: weathering and erosion; internal energy.
items.answer: For: Plate movements cause melting at subduction zones (igneous rock), metamorphism under pressure at boundaries, and uplift of rocks so they can be weathered. Against: Weathering, erosion and deposition at the surface are driven by solar energy through the water cycle and climate; sedimentary rocks form without plate activity. Judgement: Both internal (tectonic) and external (solar-driven) energy drive the cycle; plate tectonics dominate the deep processes and surface processes dominate the formation of sediments.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using named examples and data, with a reasoned judgement. Level 2 (3-5 marks): developed points but limited balance or exemplification. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generalised points. [8]

items.stem: Explain the difference in crystal size between basalt and granite.
items.answer: Basalt is extrusive and cools quickly at the surface so crystals have little time to grow; granite is intrusive and cools slowly deep underground, forming large crystals.
items.markingKey: basalt fast cooling small crystals [1]; granite slow cooling large crystals [1] [2]

items.stem: A geology student in Riyadh collected three rock samples. Sample A has large interlocking crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica. Sample B is made of rounded sand grains in layers and contains a fossil shell. Sample C has very fine grains and splits into thin flat sheets. (a) Explain how the large crystals in sample A formed. (b) Suggest how sample A might eventually become part of a sedimentary rock.
items.answer: (a) Magma cooled slowly underground, giving time for large crystals to grow. (b) It is uplifted and exposed, weathered and eroded; the sediment is transported, deposited, compacted and cemented.
items.markingKey: (a) slow cooling [1]; underground / intrusive [1] [2] (b) 1 mark per stage up to [3]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a natural event that threatens people, property or the environment”?
items.answer: Natural hazard
items.markingKey: Natural hazard: a natural event that threatens people, property or the environment. [1]

items.stem: Explain why earthquakes of similar magnitude often cause more deaths in low-income countries than in high-income countries.
items.answer: Buildings are often poorly constructed and not earthquake-resistant; emergency services and hospitals are less well equipped; there is less preparation and education; dense informal settlements; slower aid and reconstruction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed reason up to [3]

items.stem: Explain how a sea-floor earthquake can cause a tsunami.
items.answer: Sudden vertical movement of the sea bed along a fault (often at a subduction zone) displaces the overlying water column; the energy travels outwards as long-wavelength waves that slow and grow in height in shallow water near the coast.
items.markingKey: vertical displacement of sea bed [1]; water displaced [1]; waves increase in height in shallow water [1] [3]

items.stem: Refer to your case study of an earthquake or tsunami (for example the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, Nepal). Briefly evaluate the effectiveness of the management of the hazard.
items.answer: the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, Nepal: International aid and search-and-rescue teams; reconstruction slowed by poor access and governance; programmes to train builders in earthquake-resistant designs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. preparation, prediction / warning, building design, response; judgement on effectiveness [4]

items.stem: Name one example of an earthquake or tsunami you have studied and, for that example, describe the causes of the event.
items.answer: the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, Nepal: A magnitude 7.8 earthquake caused by the Indian plate colliding with and moving under the Eurasian plate along the Himalayan thrust.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. plate setting; magnitude; mechanism (sea-floor uplift, collision) [4]

items.stem: Name one example of an earthquake or tsunami you have studied and, for that example, describe the social, economic and environmental impacts.
items.answer: the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami, Japan: About 18 000 deaths, mostly drowning; about 120 000 buildings destroyed; the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power station was flooded, causing meltdowns and the evacuation of over 150 000 people; economic cost about US$235 billion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. deaths and injuries; damage; economic cost; environmental damage, with figures [4]

items.stem: Using a case study of an earthquake or tsunami, such as the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, Nepal, describe the social, economic and environmental impacts.
items.answer: Model answer (the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, Nepal): About 9000 deaths and 22 000 injuries; around 600 000 homes destroyed; avalanches on Everest and landslides blocked roads; damage to historic buildings in Kathmandu; losses equal to about a third of GDP.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: deaths and injuries; damage; economic cost; environmental damage, with figures Level 3 (5-6 marks): well-developed points on both sides with examples and a supported conclusion. Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points, limited balance or example. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple statements. [6]

items.stem: For a named example of an earthquake or tsunami that you have studied, evaluate the effectiveness of the management of the hazard.
items.answer: Model answer (the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami, Japan): Strict building codes meant few buildings collapsed from shaking; an early-warning system gave minutes of warning; drills saved many lives; but sea walls were overtopped, so later responses included higher sea walls and relocating homes to higher ground.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: preparation, prediction / warning, building design, response; judgement on effectiveness Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using place-specific detail from the named example and data, with a reasoned judgement. Level 2 (3-5 marks): developed points but limited balance or exemplification. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generalised points. [8]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a natural event that threatens people, property or the environment”?
items.answer: Natural hazard
items.markingKey: Natural hazard: a natural event that threatens people, property or the environment. [1]

items.stem: The Haiti, 2010 earthquake had a moment magnitude of 7.0 and the Christchurch, New Zealand, 2011 earthquake had a magnitude of 6.2. Deaths: Haiti, 2010 about 220 000; Christchurch, New Zealand, 2011 185. (a) Suggest reasons why the number of deaths does not simply depend on magnitude. (b) Explain why a logarithmic scale is used to measure earthquake magnitude.
items.answer: (a) Building quality and codes; population density; depth of focus and distance from cities; time of day; secondary hazards such as tsunamis and landslides; preparedness and emergency response. (b) Earthquake sizes vary over many orders of magnitude, so a logarithmic scale compresses the range into manageable numbers.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per reason up to [3] (b) wide range of sizes [1]; compresses scale [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the loose upper layer of the Earth’s surface made of mineral particles, organic matter, water and air, in which plants grow”?
items.answer: Soil
items.markingKey: Soil: the loose upper layer of the Earth’s surface made of mineral particles, organic matter, water and air, in which plants grow. [1]

items.stem: Explain how climate affects soil formation.
items.answer: Temperature and rainfall control the rate of weathering and decomposition; high rainfall causes leaching; in hot, wet climates chemical weathering is rapid but nutrients are leached; in cold climates decomposition is slow so organic matter accumulates.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed point up to [3]

items.stem: Explain why clay soils are often waterlogged.
items.answer: Clay particles are tiny and pack closely, so pore spaces are very small; water drains slowly and air is excluded.
items.markingKey: small particles / small pores [1]; slow drainage [1] [2]

items.stem: A farming cooperative on steep hillsides has seen crop yields fall by a third in ten years because of soil erosion after forest clearance. Describe the evidence of soil erosion.
items.answer: Gullies on the slopes, bare ground, muddy (high sediment) river, and falling crop yields.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per piece of evidence up to [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.4 shows a hillside farm in Rwanda where the soil has been eroded. Gullies have formed on the bare slopes and the river below has become muddy. (a) Explain why soil erosion is a problem for people living downstream. (b) Suggest why some farmers may not adopt soil conservation methods.
items.answer: (a) Sediment fills rivers and reservoirs, increasing flood risk and reducing water storage; it can damage fisheries and water quality. (b) High labour or capital cost; lack of knowledge; insecure land tenure; benefits take years to appear.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point up to [2] (b) 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: A farming cooperative on steep hillsides has seen crop yields fall by a third in ten years because of soil erosion after forest clearance. (a) Describe the evidence of soil erosion. (b) Explain why soil erosion is a problem for people living downstream.
items.answer: (a) Gullies on the slopes, bare ground, muddy (high sediment) river, and falling crop yields. (b) Sediment fills rivers and reservoirs, increasing flood risk and reducing water storage; it can damage fisheries and water quality.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per piece of evidence up to [2] (b) 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: A soil sample from a river terrace was separated by sieving and sedimentation into sand 24.5 g, silt 15.5 g and clay 10.0 g. What percentage of the sample is clay?
Which term matches this definition: “a rock containing enough of a mineral to make extraction economically worthwhile”?
items.answer: Ore
items.markingKey: Ore: a rock containing enough of a mineral to make extraction economically worthwhile. [1]

items.stem: Explain the factors that affect whether a mineral deposit is mined.
items.answer: Ore grade and size of deposit; depth and accessibility; market price and demand; extraction and transport costs; technology; environmental regulations and political stability.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor with brief explanation up to [3]

items.stem: Explain how mining can pollute water.
items.answer: Acid mine drainage releases sulfuric acid and dissolved heavy metals; tailings dams can leak or collapse; sediment from bare land increases turbidity; chemicals such as cyanide or mercury used in processing can enter rivers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: Fig. 1.5 shows land use around a large open-pit mine: the pit, spoil heaps, a tailings dam above a river, a processing plant and a new town for workers. Suggest two ways the company could reduce the environmental impact during operation.
items.answer: Line and monitor the tailings dam; treat water before release; control dust with water sprays; store topsoil for later; replant spoil heaps progressively.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per strategy up to [2]

items.stem: A company plans an open-pit copper mine in a forested valley near Bangkok. The ore grade is low and the processing plant will produce large volumes of tailings. (a) Suggest two ways the company could reduce the environmental impact during operation. (b) Suggest why local people may support the mine.
items.answer: (a) Line and monitor the tailings dam; treat water before release; control dust with water sprays; store topsoil for later; replant spoil heaps progressively. (b) Jobs, higher incomes, new roads, schools and health care, and tax revenue for the government.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per strategy up to [2] (b) 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: A company plans an open-pit copper mine in a forested valley near Kathmandu. The ore grade is low and the processing plant will produce large volumes of tailings. (a) Describe two environmental impacts of the mine. (b) Suggest why local people may support the mine.
items.answer: (a) Loss of forest habitat; dust and noise; water pollution from tailings or acid drainage; visual impact of pit and spoil; lower water table. (b) Jobs, higher incomes, new roads, schools and health care, and tax revenue for the government.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per impact up to [2] (b) 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: An open-pit zinc mine extracts 20 million tonnes of ore per year with a grade of 5% zinc. 95% of the metal in the ore is recovered by processing. For each tonne of ore, 3 tonnes of overburden must also be removed. What mass of zinc is produced per year?
Which term matches this definition: “the rigid outer shell of the Earth made of the crust and the uppermost mantle, broken into tectonic plates”?
items.answer: Lithosphere
items.markingKey: Lithosphere: the rigid outer shell of the Earth made of the crust and the uppermost mantle, broken into tectonic plates. [1]

items.stem: Explain why there are no volcanoes at a collision boundary between two continental plates.
items.answer: Neither plate is dense enough to be subducted, so no plate sinks into the mantle to melt; instead the crust is crumpled and pushed up into fold mountains.
items.markingKey: both continental / similar low density [1]; no subduction so no magma [1] [2]

items.stem: Rock samples were collected from the ocean floor on one side of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Basalt 330 km from the ridge axis has an age of 15 million years. (a) Assuming the other plate moves away at the same rate, calculate the total spreading rate across the ridge. (b) Calculate how far apart, in metres, the two plates would move in 100 000 years at this total rate.
items.answer: (a) 4.4 cm per year (b) 4400 m

items.stem: “The movement of tectonic plates is mainly caused by convection currents in the mantle.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Convection in the mantle transfers heat from the core and was the first explanation of plate motion; rising limbs coincide with ridges and sinking limbs with subduction zones. Against: Slab pull at subduction zones is now thought to be the strongest force (plates with long subducting edges, such as the Pacific plate, move fastest); ridge push also contributes. Judgement: Convection supplies the heat, but slab pull and ridge push are probably the main direct drivers of plate movement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using named examples and data, with a reasoned judgement. Level 2 (3-5 marks): developed points but limited balance or exemplification. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generalised points. [8]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “rock formed from sediments that are deposited in layers, compacted and cemented”?
items.answer: Sedimentary rock
items.markingKey: Sedimentary rock: rock formed from sediments that are deposited in layers, compacted and cemented. [1]

items.stem: Explain how metamorphic rocks form at a destructive plate boundary.
items.answer: Intense pressure from plate convergence and heat from nearby magma alter existing rocks without melting them, recrystallising minerals (regional and contact metamorphism).
items.markingKey: pressure from convergence [1]; heat from magma [1]; recrystallisation without melting [1] [3]

items.stem: A student measured mean crystal size across a basalt dyke 4 m wide. At the edge (0 m) the mean crystal size was 0.1 mm, at 1 m it was 0.4 mm and at the centre (2 m) it was 1.0 mm. Suggest how the student could make the crystal measurements more reliable.
items.answer: Measure several crystals at each distance (e.g. 10) with a hand lens and scale and calculate a mean; repeat along several lines across the intrusion.
items.markingKey: repeats / mean [1]; more sample lines [1] [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the rock cycle is mainly driven by plate tectonics.
items.answer: For: Plate movements cause melting at subduction zones (igneous rock), metamorphism under pressure at boundaries, and uplift of rocks so they can be weathered. Against: Weathering, erosion and deposition at the surface are driven by solar energy through the water cycle and climate; sedimentary rocks form without plate activity. Judgement: Both internal (tectonic) and external (solar-driven) energy drive the cycle; plate tectonics dominate the deep processes and surface processes dominate the formation of sediments.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 4 (10-12 marks): detailed, balanced evaluation supported by named examples and a clear, justified conclusion. Level 3 (7-9 marks): developed discussion with examples, judgement partly supported. Level 2 (4-6 marks): some relevant points, mostly descriptive. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, unsupported statements. [12]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “natural hazard”?
options: The point underground where an earthquake originates.
The point on the Earth’s surface directly above the focus of an earthquake.
A series of long-wavelength sea waves caused by the sudden displacement of a large volume of water, often by a sea-floor earthquake.
A natural event that threatens people, property or the environment.
items.answer: A natural event that threatens people, property or the environment.
items.markingKey: Natural hazard: a natural event that threatens people, property or the environment. [1]

items.stem: Explain why people continue to live near active volcanoes.
items.answer: Fertile volcanic soils for farming; geothermal energy; tourism; minerals; eruptions are infrequent and people may perceive the risk as low or have no alternative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per reason up to [3]

items.stem: The Gorkha, Nepal, 2015 earthquake had a moment magnitude of 7.8 and the Christchurch, New Zealand, 2011 earthquake had a magnitude of 6.2. Deaths: Gorkha, Nepal, 2015 about 9000; Christchurch, New Zealand, 2011 185. Each whole step releases about 32 times more energy (energy ∝ 10^(1.5M)). Calculate how many times more energy the larger earthquake released.

The Kashmir, Pakistan, 2005 earthquake had a moment magnitude of 7.6 and the Haiti, 2010 earthquake had a magnitude of 7.0. Deaths: Kashmir, Pakistan, 2005 about 86 000; Haiti, 2010 about 220 000. (a) Each whole step on the magnitude scale is a 10-fold increase in the amplitude of ground shaking. Calculate how many times greater the shaking was in the larger earthquake. (b) Explain why a logarithmic scale is used to measure earthquake magnitude.
items.answer: (a) 3.98 (b) Earthquake sizes vary over many orders of magnitude, so a logarithmic scale compresses the range into manageable numbers.
items.markingKey: (a) 10^0.6 [1] = 3.98 [1] [2] (b) wide range of sizes [1]; compresses scale [1] [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the impacts of earthquakes depend more on the level of development of a country than on the magnitude of the earthquake.
items.answer: For: Haiti 2010 (magnitude 7.0) killed over 200 000 people because of poor buildings and weak services, while Christchurch 2011 (6.2) killed 185. Against: Magnitude, depth and secondary hazards matter: Tōhoku 2011 (9.0) killed about 18 000 people in a high-income country because of the tsunami. Judgement: Development strongly affects vulnerability and recovery, but very large events or tsunamis can overwhelm even well-prepared countries.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using named examples and data, with a reasoned judgement. Level 2 (3-5 marks): developed points but limited balance or exemplification. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generalised points. [8]

items.stem: A student writes: “Soil is a renewable resource that forms quickly.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Soil forms very slowly (often about 1 cm in 100-1000 years), so on human timescales it is effectively non-renewable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how overgrazing leads to soil erosion.
items.answer: Animals remove the vegetation cover and trample the soil; roots no longer bind the soil and the bare surface is exposed to wind and rain, so topsoil is removed.
items.markingKey: loss of vegetation [1]; roots no longer bind / compaction [1]; exposure to wind and rain [1] [3]

items.stem: For the Sahel, West Africa or another example of soil degradation and its management, briefly explain the causes of soil degradation.
items.answer: the Sahel, West Africa: Rapid population growth, overgrazing, removal of trees for fuelwood and cultivation of marginal land, combined with droughts in the 1970s-80s, caused desertification.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. human and physical causes; processes of erosion [4]

items.stem: Fig. 1.4 shows a hillside farm in the middle hills of Nepal where the soil has been eroded. Gullies have formed on the bare slopes and the river below has become muddy. (a) Describe the evidence of soil erosion. (b) Explain why soil erosion is a problem for people living downstream. (c) Suggest why some farmers may not adopt soil conservation methods.
items.answer: (a) Gullies on the slopes, bare ground, muddy (high sediment) river, and falling crop yields. (c) High labour or capital cost; lack of knowledge; insecure land tenure; benefits take years to appear.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per piece of evidence up to [2] (b) 1 mark per point up to [2] (c) 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Open-pit mining produces less waste rock than underground mining.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Open-pit mining must remove large amounts of overburden, so it usually produces much more waste rock.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: An open-pit zinc mine extracts 100 million tonnes of ore per year with a grade of 5% zinc. 90% of the metal in the ore is recovered by processing. For each tonne of ore, 3 tonnes of overburden must also be removed. Explain why the ratio of waste to metal tends to increase over time at many mines.
items.answer: The highest-grade ore is mined first; later ore is lower grade and the pit is deeper, so more overburden must be removed per tonne of metal.
items.markingKey: declining grade [1]; deeper pit / more overburden [1] [2]

items.stem: A gold mine processes ore with a grade of 3 g of gold per tonne of ore. (a) Calculate the mass of ore that must be mined to produce 20 tonnes of gold. (b) Calculate the mass of waste produced (assume all ore except the gold becomes waste).
Which term matches this definition: “the partly molten, plastic layer of the upper mantle on which the lithospheric plates move”?
items.answer: Asthenosphere
items.markingKey: Asthenosphere: the partly molten, plastic layer of the upper mantle on which the lithospheric plates move. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Oceanic crust is younger than most continental crust.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Oceanic crust is recycled by subduction and is rarely older than about 200 million years, while continental crust can be over 4 billion years old.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Rock samples were collected from the ocean floor on one side of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Basalt 600 km from the ridge axis has an age of 25 million years. (a) Assuming the other plate moves away at the same rate, calculate the total spreading rate across the ridge. (b) Suggest one reason why the calculated rate is only an estimate.
items.answer: (a) 4.8 cm per year (b) The rate may not have been constant over time; dating and distance measurements have errors; only one sample was used.

items.stem: Fig. 1.1 is a cross-section across the west coast of South America, showing the Nazca plate moving east towards the South American plate, an ocean trench, and the Andes mountains with volcanoes. (a) Name the type of plate boundary shown. (b) Explain why an ocean trench forms at this boundary. (c) Explain the formation of the volcanoes. (d) Describe how the mountains were formed.
items.answer: (a) Destructive (convergent, subduction) boundary. (b) The denser oceanic plate bends down and sinks beneath the continental plate, creating a deep trench where it descends. (c) The subducted plate is heated at depth and releases water; mantle melts; magma rises through the continental crust and erupts. (d) Compression as the plates converge folds and thickens the continental crust, and volcanic material adds to it, forming fold mountains.

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “rock formed when existing rock is changed by heat and/or pressure without melting”?
items.answer: Metamorphic rock
items.markingKey: Metamorphic rock: rock formed when existing rock is changed by heat and/or pressure without melting. [1]

items.stem: Outline one similarity and two differences between granite and basalt.
items.answer: Differences: Granite is intrusive with large crystals and is pale and silica-rich; basalt is extrusive with small crystals and is dark and iron-rich. Similarity: Both are igneous rocks made of interlocking crystals.
items.markingKey: 1 mark similarity; 1 mark per comparative difference up to 2 [3]

items.stem: A geology student in Lisbon collected three rock samples. Sample A has large interlocking crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica. Sample B is made of rounded sand grains in layers and contains a fossil shell. Sample C has very fine grains and splits into thin flat sheets. Describe how sample C could have formed from a sedimentary rock.
items.answer: Shale or mudstone was subjected to high pressure (and heat), e.g. at a plate boundary; minerals realigned in parallel, so it splits into sheets (slate).
items.markingKey: pressure / heat [1]; realignment / cleavage [1] [2]

items.stem: Mei examined three rocks during fieldwork: rock A (coarse crystals, no layers), rock B (layered grains with fossils) and rock C (fine-grained, splits into flat sheets). (a) Identify the type of rock for each sample. (b) Explain how the large crystals in sample A formed. (c) Explain why sample B contains fossils. (d) Describe how sample C could have formed from a sedimentary rock. (e) Suggest how sample A might eventually become part of a sedimentary rock.
items.answer: (a) A igneous (intrusive, e.g. granite); B sedimentary (e.g. sandstone or limestone); C metamorphic (e.g. slate). (b) Magma cooled slowly underground, giving time for large crystals to grow. (c) It formed from sediment deposited in layers, which buried organisms; low temperatures preserved their remains, which were lithified with the sediment. (d) Shale or mudstone was subjected to high pressure (and heat), e.g. at a plate boundary; minerals realigned in parallel, so it splits into sheets (slate). (e) It is uplifted and exposed, weathered and eroded; the sediment is transported, deposited, compacted and cemented.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) slow cooling [1]; underground / intrusive [1] [2] (c) deposition burying organisms [1]; no melting / preserved [1] [2] (d) pressure / heat [1]; realignment / cleavage [1] [2] (e) 1 mark per stage up to [3]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “focus (hypocentre)”?
options: A series of long-wavelength sea waves caused by the sudden displacement of a large volume of water, often by a sea-floor earthquake.
The point on the Earth’s surface directly above the focus of an earthquake.
A fast-moving, very hot cloud of ash, gas and rock fragments that flows down the side of a volcano.
The point underground where an earthquake originates.
items.answer: The point underground where an earthquake originates.
items.markingKey: Focus (hypocentre): the point underground where an earthquake originates. [1]

items.stem: Describe how volcanic eruptions can be predicted.
items.answer: Monitoring small earthquakes (seismometers), ground deformation (tiltmeters, GPS, satellite radar), increased gas emissions such as sulfur dioxide, and rising ground temperature.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per method up to [3]

items.stem: Tsunami waves travel at a speed given by v = √(g × d), where g = 9.8 m/s² and d is the ocean depth in metres. A tsunami crosses ocean of average depth 4 000 m towards Galle in Sri Lanka, 2 000 km from the epicentre. Explain why the waves increase in height as they approach the coast.
items.answer: In shallow water the waves slow down, so the wavelength shortens and the water piles up, increasing wave height.
items.markingKey: slow down in shallow water [1]; energy concentrated / height increases [1] [2]

items.stem: Tsunami waves travel at a speed given by v = √(g × d), where g = 9.8 m/s² and d is the ocean depth in metres. A tsunami crosses ocean of average depth 5 000 m towards Banda Aceh, 500 km from the epicentre. (a) Explain why the waves increase in height as they approach the coast. (b) Use your answer to explain the importance of an early warning system.
items.answer: (a) In shallow water the waves slow down, so the wavelength shortens and the water piles up, increasing wave height. (b) There are only about 37.6 minutes before the waves arrive, so rapid detection and communication are needed for people to evacuate to higher ground.
items.markingKey: (a) slow down in shallow water [1]; energy concentrated / height increases [1] [2] (b) uses time [1]; evacuation linked [1] [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that it is more effective to prepare for volcanic eruptions than to respond after them. In your answer you should consider: named volcanoes; evacuation.
items.answer: For: Monitoring at Mount Pinatubo (1991) allowed evacuation of about 60 000 people and saved thousands of lives; hazard maps and land-use zoning reduce exposure. Against: Prediction is uncertain and costly; evacuations disrupt lives (Montserrat 1995-97); response, aid and recovery are still essential after any eruption. Judgement: Preparation reduces loss of life most cost-effectively, but must be combined with an effective response and recovery plan.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using named examples and data, with a reasoned judgement. Level 2 (3-5 marks): developed points but limited balance or exemplification. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generalised points. [8]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Removing vegetation increases the risk of soil erosion.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Plant cover intercepts rain and roots bind the soil; without it soil is exposed to wind and rain splash.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why organic matter is important for soil fertility.
items.answer: Humus releases nutrients as it decomposes, holds water and nutrients, improves soil structure and aeration, and supports soil organisms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: A soil sample from a river terrace was separated by sieving and sedimentation into sand 44.0 g, silt 43.0 g and clay 13.0 g. (a) A 57.1 g sample of dry soil was heated strongly and its mass fell to 54.5 g. Calculate the percentage organic matter. (b) Explain how the texture of this soil will affect its drainage and fertility.
items.answer: (a) 4.6% (b) A balanced mixture gives good drainage and aeration while holding water and nutrients, so it is fertile.
items.markingKey: (a) (57.1 − 54.5) ÷ 57.1 × 100 [1] = 4.6% [1] [2] (b) drainage linked to particle / pore size [1]; fertility linked [1] [2]

items.stem: A farming cooperative on steep hillsides has seen crop yields fall by a third in ten years because of soil erosion after forest clearance. (a) Describe the evidence of soil erosion. (b) Explain why soil erosion is a problem for people living downstream. (c) Suggest why some farmers may not adopt soil conservation methods.
items.answer: (a) Gullies on the slopes, bare ground, muddy (high sediment) river, and falling crop yields. (b) Sediment fills rivers and reservoirs, increasing flood risk and reducing water storage; it can damage fisheries and water quality. (c) High labour or capital cost; lack of knowledge; insecure land tenure; benefits take years to appear.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per piece of evidence up to [2] (b) 1 mark per point up to [2] (c) 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Mining can bring economic benefits to a region.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It creates jobs, tax revenue and export earnings, and can lead to new infrastructure such as roads.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.5 shows land use around a large open-pit mine: the pit, spoil heaps, a tailings dam above a river, a processing plant and a new town for workers. Suggest why local people may support the mine.
items.answer: Jobs, higher incomes, new roads, schools and health care, and tax revenue for the government.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: An open-pit copper mine extracts 100 million tonnes of ore per year with a grade of 0.4% copper. 85% of the metal in the ore is recovered by processing. For each tonne of ore, 3 tonnes of overburden must also be removed. (a) Explain why the ratio of waste to metal tends to increase over time at many mines. (b) Suggest one way the waste could be managed to reduce environmental impacts.
items.answer: (a) The highest-grade ore is mined first; later ore is lower grade and the pit is deeper, so more overburden must be removed per tonne of metal. (b) Store tailings in lined, monitored dams or as dry stacks; use overburden to backfill and restore the pit; cover sulfide waste to prevent acid drainage.
items.markingKey: (a) declining grade [1]; deeper pit / more overburden [1] [2] (b) [1]
